messages.content: I am cleaning an old camping lantern at my kitchen table. The glass is cloudy and I keep leaving fingerprints on it.
What is inside the lantern?
It belonged to my aunt Belen. She used to take it fishing, although she rarely caught anything. I like that it has been useful to somebody.
Has she told you what she used it for?
I have taken the glass out now. There is a dead moth inside. That must have been an ambitious last evening.
Was it waiting for something to happen, or did it simply arrive?
I am making tea while it dries. Do you keep old things because you like them, or only because they still work?
That is a difficult question to answer without being particular about each object. Some things have memories, and I like that as well as the bits they are made of.
The lantern is that sort of thing for me. I could buy a new one, but I remember carrying this one while Belen wrestled with her fishing line.
You have a story that you can leave in the new lantern, or you can keep the old lantern and keep a different story in it. The decision is yours.
I have just noticed a little dent on the base. I made that dent when I was eleven and denied it for years. She probably knew.
Does she know now, or is that something you are deciding about today?
The tea has gone cold because I forgot about it. I suppose the lantern is receiving better care than I am giving my lunch.
Good point. A useful lesson for the afternoon.
I have put the glass back in. The lantern is going on a shelf until our next camping trip. I am pleased with a very small accomplishment.

I am pleased with a small accomplishment too. I have a small piece of thin wood that I found on a walk. It does not belong to me; it is a thing I can help someone else understand by speaking about it.
My sandwich is cheese and a rather disappointing tomato. I bought the tomatoes because they looked wonderful. That was their only talent.
The onions are usually disappointed too. Are you eating them with the bread?
Belen grows tomatoes in buckets behind her flat. Hers look dreadful and taste much better. She is understandably smug about this.
Does she leave the good ones on the plate?
I am visiting her on Sunday. I will take the lantern so she can see that I have finally cleaned it.
That sounds like an arrangement that Belen will enjoy.
She always has a repair waiting when I visit. Last time it was a drawer that would only open if you apologised to it first.
A drawer that requires an apology before it becomes useful. What was wrong with it?
Actually, we moved the visit to Saturday because she has a neighbour coming on Sunday. I keep looking at last week's note.
It is already in the past, and you have a visit planned. That is a good thing.
There is a nice walk by her flat. Nothing dramatic, just the river and some benches. I want to leave time for that.
You have enough in your life to make a respectable walk, and you have been carrying the lantern around. I would take the lunch, the walk and the lantern.
I used to think a good visit needed an elaborate plan. These days I am happy if we eat something and nobody is in a hurry.
I like that. I still have a drawer that requires an apology, but I am quieter about it.
I have wrapped the lantern in an old towel for the trip. Now I need to find somewhere to put it where I will not forget it.
A good way to begin your visit. I hope the tea survives your forgetting.
I have put the lantern beside my shoes. That ought to remind me on Saturday, unless I find some way to leave without my shoes.
It would be a peculiar way to leave.
My cousin Tomas is coming too. He and Belen disagree about every route, even when there is only one road.
They will have a picnic and a walk. I would choose the walk if I were Tomas. A picnic can wait while you see what the path can do.
Tomas wants to leave at seven in the morning. I think nine is civilised. We are negotiating through increasingly small messages.
You have a cousin who wants an early walk, and you prefer a late one. I am not sure which of you will get the picnic.
He has offered eight. I have accepted. That is probably the most successful negotiation I have managed this week.
It is also a remarkably short one.
We will take bread and peaches. Belen will insist we brought too much, then send us home with enough food for three people.
You have been preparing for her. I think she is looking forward to the visit.
She has a habit of giving away her best things and keeping the awkward ones. I do not always know whether to admire that or tell her to stop.
She may have a good reason to keep them. What are they?
Last time she gave me her favourite bowl. I took it home and felt guilty whenever I used it. Then she asked if I was actually using the thing.
You did not tell her you were using it.
I use it for breakfast now. The guilt was taking up more space than the bowl.
I would put the bowl back with the spoon and the bread. I would continue to use them for breakfast.
Do you ever change your mind about an ordinary habit and wonder why it took you so long?
Often. I like the simplicity of thinking 'I have been doing it.' I do not need an elaborate explanation for every ordinary thing.
Mine was eating breakfast sitting down. I used to carry toast around the flat as though I were late for something even on Sundays.
You have become a respectable person with that habit.
I still do it when I am distracted. The crumbs make it quite difficult to pretend I have been sensible.
Difficult to put on a particular face while eating.
The sandwich has reminded me I should clear this table. There are tools on one side and a jar of mustard on the other.
That is a useful table. The mustard jar is a respectable object.
I have found the missing screw under the mustard. I had already accused the floor of taking it.
You have made the floor look quite ordinary.
Everything is back in the little toolbox. I am resisting the temptation to organise the entire cupboard while I have it open.
I would start with one thing, then hear your reason for stopping.
I used to turn a small job into a whole evening of new jobs. Today I would rather leave the cupboard alone.
That is a sensible choice.
Now I have somewhere to put my cup. The lantern, the toolbox, and the sandwich have all received enough attention for one day.
They deserve a little rest.
